items.title: Show HN: Flowmaps – the logic layer for agents and developers
items.description:
Show HN: Hi everyone, I've spent the last few months building a tool called Flowmaps. It's the logic layer for agents and developers. It sits between your team and your codebase and constantly builds and maintains a logical map of what the code does. Agents are already writing a large volume of code. The bottleneck has become the process of understanding what it does. Agents don't make the same mistakes that programmers do; instead the errors are usually related to logic that the agent doesn't have full context on. Flowmaps helps you understand the what the code does without having to read it line-by-line. For developers, this means reviewing and understanding agent PRs without losing touch with the code. Agents also share an understanding of the code in a way that ensures consistency and less token spend across the organization. I'm looking for some early users to try it out for free and provide some feedback. If you're interested, add yourself to the waitlist or send an email to [email removed]. Thanks!
Website metadata: Map every flow in your codebase into plain-language steps backed by cited code, kept current with every pull request. Built for developers and AI agents.

items.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN! I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious. So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves. I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging ( https://declarative-dragging.github.io/ ) on the front page of HN and the spark came back! It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions. A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance
Website metadata: Algebra you do with your hands: drag any part of an equation, and it only moves the ways the maths allows. Lessons, practice and teachers' own exercise sets.
items.product_description: Algebra you do with your hands: drag any part of an equation, and it only moves the ways the maths allows. Lessons, practice and teachers' own exercise sets.

items.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
items.description:
Show HN: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

items.title: Show HN: Open-Sourced Code Mode to Cut ~60% of My Rust Agent's Token Burn
items.description:
Show HN: For those who are tracking, Anthropic released an announcement last week about their experimental code mode for Claude Code, claiming some bonkers token savings when it comes to tool calls (95% on some workloads(1)). I haven't benchmarked it myself, but independent studies come in somewhere closer to 60~70% savings (2), but I digress. TLDR; I built an open-source version for the community. Context: I'm writing an AI RPG engine called Spookery, and I immediately wanted to try this technique for myself when I heard of it. Agent deployment is currently dominated by token costs, especially during tool calling (single prompt generating tens or hundreds of tool calls). Unfortunately, it looks like the only ones who are doing this seriously are big agentic products like Claude Code and Codex. So, I thought it'd be fun to try it myself and bring it to you all! The idea of Code Mode is simple but powerful. Instead of passing back tool call results back to the LLM one at a time, let the LLM batch calls by letting it write a short script using your tools. Basically taking 30 trips to the grocery store for 30 items and turning it into one trip to the store with a list in-hand. There's a few near-ish open-source options, but they used TypeScript backends, we're a little boilerplate heavy, and I wanted to have something a little faster and Rust friendly for my game engine. Pydantic's Monty seemed a good candidate--their self-reports are around 5x faster on execution and 100x faster on startup (3). I wouldn't take the numbers to the bank, but it's written on a Rust framework and the python backend is entirely built from Rust too. Anyway, I had a couple of days off unexpectedly. So, I went temporarily insane and built a Rust tool to bring code mode to the greater community for free. In enough days to fit on one hand (and just as many hours of sleep), I came up with the implementation linked. I call it Ghost Mode. It's MIT licensed. It's a drop-in for your agent that already makes traditional tool calls. With ~20 lines of setup, you can convert your existing agent to a Code Mode agent. I hope you get something out of this, and maybe I can save you some money. Considering how limiting token economics are right now, I think this could be a game changer for the industry. If there's interest, I can imagine we can build also add some great new features, language compatibility, and other great things. Thanks for reading :) Sources: (1) https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/17/ant
Website metadata: Code Mode for Rust agents: sandboxed execute and poll tools for agentic REPL loops. - legend-of-alan/ghostmode
items.product_description: Code Mode for Rust agents: sandboxed execute and poll tools for agentic REPL loops. - legend-of-alan/ghostmode

items.title: Show HN: Play with VST/CLAP instruments and effects in the browser
items.description: Show HN: For awhile now, I thought it'd be cool to be able to try out various instrument / effect plugins in the browser without having to download them and open up a DAW. I saw this as a challenge, so I spent the last few weeks working on a demo app. One thing I wanted to avoid was making this obscenely costly. Plugins can be CPU and memory intensive, so larger EC2 instances would be needed. However, running even one of these continuously is very expensive, let alone a fleet of them. I initially tried working with a single instance and attempting a sort of preemptive scheduling / context switching, but this quickly fell apart: the signal chain between sessions would become polluted, and it was extremely brittle. It's around this time that I found that EC2 spot instances can be considerably cheaper. With aggressive session cleanup and instance lifetime limits, I could probably keep this doable. Limitations: * Max session time is an hour. * Only a single signal chain is supported, with an instrument being the root node and one or more effects after it. Parallel chains are technically supported by the engine, but I decided against implementing it in the browser for simplicity. * Plugins marked with "demo" are paid products with a publicly available demo version. These demos will emit crackles or dropouts, so if you like the plugin, consider purchasing it from the developer. * Snapshots allow you to freeze your graph (plugin order, parameter values) at a specific time, and also share your snapshot with others. Currently, snapshots are stored in memory only, as I didn't want to over engineer a durable store for a demo app. Also, once your session is over, snapshots are deleted along with it. * Some plugins may work better than others. Implementation details: * Sessions provision EC2 spot instances, or grab hibernating instances from a pool if one is available. * Each EC2 instance runs a worker binary that maintains a graph of nodes, with each node being a Podman container that communicates with the worker via Unix sockets. * Podman images include WINE and yabridge for VST3 only plugins; container initialization time is kept low thanks to fuse-overlayfs preventing redundant copying of the WINE prefix. * Each container has a small VST/CLAP host that reads input via the control socket; output can be GUI frames or audio blocks. * Output is streamed over a WebSocket, with WebAudio for scheduling playback

items.title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow. I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all. SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders: - Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads) - Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library) Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/. A couple of caveats up front: - Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy. - macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices). It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew: brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop Just sharing in case others run into the same friction—feedback or PRs welcome!
Website metadata: Drag files into iOS simulators from the Finder sidebar - rxliuli/sim-drop
items.product_description: Drag files into iOS simulators from the Finder sidebar - rxliuli/sim-drop
